body.text: Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
You could fill more than a couple of backpacks with all the backtracks the government has been doing of late — and this time it was Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke's turn.
The Labor stalwart smiled as he did his best to spin his changes to the changes on backpacker policy.

He back-pedalled on plans to slash the numbers of working holiday maker visas and lifted a proposed cap on third-year visas, while also increasing the number of days foreigners must work in the regions to be eligible.

He also delayed the introduction of a ballot system until March, and it has now been rebranded as a "ballot-style" system called the Next Year Regional Work Guarantee, after pressure from the agriculture, tourism and hospitality sectors.

Burke argued a go-slow to visa processing earlier this year gave him the headroom to make the tweaks, insisting it wouldn't impact the guarantee he made back in September that the government was definitely going to reduce Australia's net overseas migration. In other words, Labor is on track to achieve its targets because Home Affairs is processing visas really, really slowly.

Of course, the government would argue it's hardly uncommon to change its position. As Murray Watt argued when pressed on the backpacker visa changes: "You put out a proposal, you then talk about it with the stakeholders, and you arrive at a final landing spot, and that's what we've been able to do here."
Others, such as Greens leader David Shoebridge, argued that's a back-to-front approach.

"I've got some advice for the government: maybe before you have your next brain fart, go out and talk to the community, see who's going to be impacted and do that before you make the announcement," he said.

The backpacker backtrack is not the first. The Albanese government has been quick to shelve issues before they become too much of a political problem. There's been the scrapping of the veterans' allied health cap, the ATO credit card ban, the sale of four defence sites, just to name a few over recent months.
But all of this chopping and changing does have an impact on the budget bottom line — something the government has its eyes on as the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook draws closer.
Trusts and the guillotine

Treasurer Jim Chalmers returned to the spotlight this week after a fortnight in the dark (I mean this literally — he posted a video of himself driving around in the dark to Instagram after storms hit his electorate).

Chalmers delivered a speech to an ASIC forum where he repeated much of what he's already said: there will be savings in the budget. As reporters questioned him, he also insisted he would remain treasurer until the next election.

The budget headaches go beyond just MYEFO for Chalmers as the status of his budget tax changes — the capital gains discount and a minimum 30 per cent tax on discretionary trusts — continues to be a thorn in the government's side.

Neither were dealt with during the Senate-only sitting week. When the guillotine motion — which cuts off debate to force votes on a number of bills — was put forward on Thursday afternoon, it was clear a deal was still yet to be done.

The Coalition remains "dead against" both. So that leaves the Greens as the only path forward. The minor party floated the idea of sending the CGT changes off to yet another inquiry as it publicly flirted with Allegra Spender's alternative idea.

If the CGT changes did go to an inquiry, that would delay its passage until next year — something the government really doesn't want. It's likely the Greens will end up passing both bills next week with some amendments.
Cook-ing with gas (reservation scheme)

Between the casting of James Bond (spare a thought for Don Farrell, who seemed willing to trade his moniker as the Godfather for Bond), the release of GTA 6 and Sandpapergate, if your attention wasn't on the Senate only sitting week… that's so fair.
So, what happened? Not much.

The tax bills weren't dealt with, and neither was the gas reservation scheme. The proposal would require Australia's largest gas exports to set aside up to 20 per cent of its exports for domestic supply. An unlikely alliance of unions and industry groups called for the parliament to pass it this week.

Western Australia had been the big sticking point here. The state has its own scheme set up and has been arguing for a carve-out to be baked in, rather than through ministerial discretion. Premier Roger Cook (it's always him, hey), struck a last-minute deal.

All eyes are now on the Coalition. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor indicated early in the week that WA was the key block to the party's support. But other conditions include greater limits on ministerial powers, concerns about deliberate oversupply and the removal of the "must sell" rule on producers.
It also wasn't put up for a vote on Thursday, dragging the issue into next week alongside CGT, trusts, and private health insurance rebate changes.
Pom-pom and ceremony
What do a chicken shop in Manila and rows of pom-pom wielding cheerleaders have in common? Anthony Albanese.

The prime minister headed overseas again. This time his schedule took him to the Philippines for ASEAN, where the Quad leaders — which includes US President Donald Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi — met for the first time in two years.
Trump's assessment of the group? Modi was "a very tough man" but Takaichi "may be even tougher". As for the PM, well, "We're okay," he said before giving him a slap on the back.
An agreement to conduct a joint military exercise and to cooperate on critical minerals were the key takeaways from the meeting that took place before they jetted off to APEC in Shenzhen, China.

While Albanese was greeted by cheerleaders, President Xi Jinping welcomed Trump with a hug on the tarmac. The pair will be joined by Russian President Vladmir Putin for a trilateral meeting on Thursday afternoon.
Ahead of the meeting, Albanese called the dialogue a "good thing".
"At a time when there are more conflicts than at any time since the Second World War … we want to see more dialogue, less military conflict," he said.
The PM is set to have his own talks with Xi on the sidelines of APEC on Friday. It'll act as a primer for talks when parliament returns next week for the final sitting week of the year.
